findings.description: `requestReset` calls `mailer.sendPin` inside its database transaction, before the pending token write has committed. If SMTP accepts the message but the transaction subsequently fails during flush or commit, the delivered PIN has no database record and every verification attempt rejects it.

evidence.explanation: The service method is transactional, saves the token, and then performs synchronous SMTP delivery before returning; verification later requires that token to exist in the database.

fix_suggestion.fix_description: Send mail only after token commit
fix_suggestion.prompt_to_fix:
## Issue description
The reset email is sent before the transaction that stores its token commits, so a commit failure can leave users with a PIN that cannot be verified.

## Fix Focus Areas
- sample_project_BE/src/main/java/com/sampleproject/diary/service/PasswordResetService.java[56-77]
- sample_project_BE/src/main/java/com/sampleproject/diary/service/PasswordResetMailer.java[48-82]

## Recommended Fix
Publish the reset-mail work only after the token transaction commits, using an after-commit transactional event or a transactional outbox. Ensure a failed database commit sends no email, while preserving explicit handling and observability for post-commit SMTP failures.

findings.title: Emailed reset codes may never work

findings.description: `PasswordResetProperties` binds the reset lifetime, attempt limit, and development PIN without validating any of them. A nonpositive lifetime or attempt limit makes every new token immediately unusable, while a development PIN outside the accepted digit format can be generated but never submitted successfully.

evidence.explanation: The configuration record has no validation annotations, while the service directly uses these values to calculate expiration and token usability and the request DTOs only accept four-to-eight decimal digits.

fix_suggestion.prompt_to_fix:
## Issue description
Password-reset environment settings are accepted without constraints, allowing validly parsed but unusable values to disable account recovery at runtime.

## Fix Focus Areas
- sample_project_BE/src/main/java/com/sampleproject/diary/security/PasswordResetProperties.java[13-15]
- sample_project_BE/src/main/resources/application.yml[59-67]

## Recommended Fix
Enable configuration-property validation and require positive values for the PIN lifetime and attempt limit. Require the development PIN to match the same 4-to-8 digit format accepted by the reset request DTOs so invalid deployments fail clearly during startup.

findings.title: Bad settings disable password recovery

findings.description: `PasswordResetToken` introduces the `password_reset_tokens` table, but this PR provides neither a schema migration nor a migration tool dependency that can create it. When an existing production database uses the documented `JPA_DDL_AUTO=validate` setting, Hibernate validates the new entity mapping against the unchanged schema and aborts application startup before reset requests can be served.

evidence.explanation: The new entity explicitly maps a previously absent table and the reset repository queries it. The only resource file is `application.yml`; the README instructs production to use Hibernate validation and migrations, while the build has no Flyway/Liquibase dependency or migration resources, so an existing validated schema cannot gain the required table.

fix_suggestion.prompt_to_fix:
Issue description
The new `password_reset_tokens` entity requires a database table and index, but no production schema migration accompanies it. Deployments configured with Hibernate validation cannot start against an existing database that lacks this table.

Fix Focus Areas
- sample_project_BE/src/main/java/com/sampleproject/diary/entity/PasswordResetToken.java[28-31]
- sample_project_BE/pom.xml[24-96]

Recommended Fix
Add and configure the repository's chosen migration mechanism, then include a versioned migration that creates `password_reset_tokens` with its UUID primary key, `user_id` foreign key, token fields, and the `user_id` index declared by the entity. Ensure migrations run before Hibernate schema validation in production.

introduced.title: Production deployments fail to start

still_open.description: `generatePin` returns the configured development PIN whenever mail credentials are blank, while the supplied configuration defaults those credentials to blank and the PIN to `1234`. In the documented Docker deployment, anyone who knows an account email can request a token and submit that public value to replace the password without mailbox access.

evidence.explanation: Mail credentials default to empty values, `generatePin` substitutes `properties.devPin()` when they are empty, and all reset endpoints are publicly accessible. Docker Compose also defaults the development PIN to `1234`, making the full takeover path available in the default deployment.

fix_suggestion.prompt_to_fix:
## Issue description
Password resets silently use the predictable PIN `1234` whenever mail credentials are absent, allowing account takeover in the default deployment.

## Fix Focus Areas
- sample_project_BE/src/main/resources/application.yml[59-67]
- sample_project_BE/docker-compose.yml[38-45]
- sample_project_BE/src/main/java/com/sampleproject/diary/service/PasswordResetService.java[134-142]

## Recommended Fix
Remove the fixed production fallback and fail startup when mail is unavailable unless an explicit development-only profile is active. Keep any development PIN behavior confined to that profile and require an explicit, non-default value.

still_open.title: Known reset PINs enable takeovers

still_open.description: `PasswordResetMailer.sendPin` catches SMTP failures and writes the destination email and still-valid PIN to the application error log. Because `requestReset` persists the token before sending mail, anyone with access to centralized or container logs can use that credential to replace the account password.

evidence.explanation: The token is saved before `sendPin` runs, and the exception handler logs both its PIN and recipient at an enabled error level. The reset service subsequently accepts that same PIN to update the user's password.

fix_suggestion.prompt_to_fix:
## Issue description
SMTP failures expose valid password-reset credentials and account email addresses in application logs.

## Fix Focus Areas
- sample_project_BE/src/main/java/com/sampleproject/diary/service/PasswordResetMailer.java[72-81]
- sample_project_BE/src/main/java/com/sampleproject/diary/service/PasswordResetService.java[68-77]

## Recommended Fix
Remove the PIN and recipient address from failure logs, log only a non-sensitive correlation identifier, and invalidate the persisted token or return a controlled delivery failure when sending does not succeed.

still_open.title: Mail failures expose live reset PINs

still_open.description: `consumeToken` checks token state and marks it consumed through separate read and write operations without a database lock or optimistic version field. Concurrent requests carrying the same valid PIN can both pass the usability check and overwrite the password, while concurrent wrong guesses can also lose attempt increments and exceed the configured limit.

evidence.explanation: The repository performs an ordinary lookup, the entity has no `@Version` field, and the service checks fields before separately saving their modifications. Thus multiple transactions can observe the same original `consumedAt` and `attempts` values.

fix_suggestion.prompt_to_fix:
## Issue description
Concurrent reset requests can reuse a supposedly single-use PIN, and concurrent failed guesses can bypass the attempt budget through lost updates.

## Fix Focus Areas
- sample_project_BE/src/main/java/com/sampleproject/diary/service/PasswordResetService.java[108-130]
- sample_project_BE/src/main/java/com/sampleproject/diary/repository/PasswordResetTokenRepository.java[14-21]
- sample_project_BE/src/main/java/com/sampleproject/diary/entity/PasswordResetToken.java[58-63]

## Recommended Fix
Load the token under a pessimistic write lock or use a versioned/conditional atomic update that succeeds only while it is unconsumed, unexpired, and below the attempt limit. Update the password only after exactly one transaction successfully claims the token, and atomically increment failed attempts.

still_open.title: One PIN can change a password twice

still_open.description: `forgotPassword` exposes `requestReset` publicly without an account cooldown, source limit, or other throttling control. Repeated requests for a victim perform password hashing, replace the current PIN, and send another SMTP message, allowing unauthenticated callers to consume resources and continuously invalidate the victim's emailed PIN.

evidence.explanation: Security configuration permits the endpoint without authentication, and every accepted request for an existing account creates a BCrypt hash, deletes the previous token, persists a replacement, and invokes the mail sender. No rate-limiting or cooldown check occurs in that path.

fix_suggestion.prompt_to_fix:
## Issue description
The public password-reset request endpoint permits unlimited expensive hashing, token replacement, and email delivery for arbitrary accounts.

## Fix Focus Areas
- sample_project_BE/src/main/java/com/sampleproject/diary/controller/AuthController.java[71-85]
- sample_project_BE/src/main/java/com/sampleproject/diary/service/PasswordResetService.java[55-77]
- sample_project_BE/src/main/java/com/sampleproject/diary/config/SecurityConfig.java[25-35]

## Recommended Fix
Add server-side limits by source address and normalized account identifier, plus a per-account resend cooldown enforced before hashing or SMTP work. Preserve the generic success response when a request is limited so registration status is not disclosed.

still_open.title: Attackers can flood reset emails

still_open.description: `resetPassword` changes only `User.passwordHash` and does not advance any session or token-revocation state. A JWT stolen before the password change therefore continues authenticating to diary endpoints until its normal expiration, even after the owner completes account recovery.

evidence.explanation: The reset transaction only updates the password hash, while generated JWTs contain no revocation version and the authentication filter performs no password-change or revocation comparison. Previously issued signed tokens consequently remain accepted.

fix_suggestion.prompt_to_fix:
## Issue description
Existing bearer tokens remain usable after password recovery, allowing an attacker with a stolen session to retain account access.

## Fix Focus Areas
- sample_project_BE/src/main/java/com/sampleproject/diary/service/PasswordResetService.java[92-101]
- sample_project_BE/src/main/java/com/sampleproject/diary/security/JwtService.java[28-40]
- sample_project_BE/src/main/java/com/sampleproject/diary/security/JwtAuthenticationFilter.java[38-44]

## Recommended Fix
Store a password-change timestamp or token version on the user, include the corresponding issue state in new JWTs, and reject tokens issued before the latest password reset. Advance that state in the same transaction that changes the password.

still_open.title: Stolen sessions survive a reset

still_open.description: `requestReset` returns immediately after lookup for an unknown email but performs BCrypt hashing, database writes, and synchronous SMTP delivery for a registered email. Although the response bodies match, callers can repeatedly measure the large account-dependent latency difference to determine which addresses are registered.

evidence.explanation: Unknown addresses take only the repository lookup and branch directly to return, whereas known addresses additionally execute BCrypt encoding, deletion, insertion, and synchronous mail delivery before the controller responds. SMTP timeouts are configured up to five seconds, making that latency distinction externally observable.

fix_suggestion.prompt_to_fix:
## Issue description
Account-dependent work makes password-reset response latency reveal whether an email address is registered despite the generic response body.

## Fix Focus Areas
- sample_project_BE/src/main/java/com/sampleproject/diary/service/PasswordResetService.java[55-77]
- sample_project_BE/src/main/java/com/sampleproject/diary/controller/AuthController.java[71-85]

## Recommended Fix
Move account lookup, token generation, and mail delivery to an asynchronous worker so the HTTP request returns before account-dependent processing. Combine this with request throttling and keep observable status, body, and response timing independent of whether the account exists.

still_open.title: Timing reveals registered accounts

still_open.description: `findByEmailIgnoreCase` returns a single `Optional<User>`, but registration’s case-sensitive `existsByEmail` check and the ordinary database uniqueness constraint allow multiple accounts whose addresses differ only by letter case. Once case variants exist, the case-insensitive lookup can throw a multiple-results data-access exception during both reset PIN issuance and consumption, which reaches the global handler as HTTP 500.

diff_reference.code_snippet:
+    /** Case-insensitive: emails are stored as typed, but looked up as entered. */
+    Optional<User> findByEmailIgnoreCase(String email);

evidence.explanation: The repository adds a case-insensitive email query with a single-result return type and the password-reset flow uses it directly. Registration checks the submitted email case-sensitively, while the entity and database provide only ordinary email uniqueness rather than normalized or case-insensitive uniqueness, so case-variant rows can coexist; querying those rows through the new method is therefore ambiguous, and unexpected repository exceptions are mapped to HTTP 500.

fix_suggestion.prompt_to_fix:
## Issue description
Password reset uses a case-insensitive single-result email lookup, while registration and database uniqueness remain case-sensitive and allow multiple accounts whose addresses differ only by case. Make account identity consistently case-insensitive and prevent case-variant duplicates.

## Fix Focus Areas
- sample_project_BE/src/main/java/com/sampleproject/diary/repository/UserRepository.java[13-18]
- sample_project_BE/src/main/java/com/sampleproject/diary/service/PasswordResetService.java[57-63]
- sample_project_BE/src/main/java/com/sampleproject/diary/service/AuthService.java[37-47]
- sample_project_BE/src/main/java/com/sampleproject/diary/entity/User.java[24-29]

## Recommended Fix
Choose one canonical email representation, such as trimming and lowercasing with `Locale.ROOT`, and apply it consistently before registration checks, persistence, and password-reset lookups. Add an appropriate PostgreSQL schema migration that enforces database-level uniqueness over the normalized value, and migrate or resolve any existing case-colliding records before adding the constraint.

still_open.title: Case-variant accounts cannot reset

still_open.description: `submitPassword` handles every reset failure by setting `formError` while retaining `step === 'password'`, even though its own comment says a burned or expired PIN requires starting over. When a PIN expires after verification or is superseded before submission, every retry uses the same captured PIN and the screen provides no control back to the email or PIN step.

evidence.explanation: The final request always submits the PIN stored before entering the password step, while its catch block changes only the error message. The password-step markup contains password fields and a submit button but no way to request or enter another PIN, and the backend permanently rejects expired, consumed, or superseded tokens.

fix_suggestion.prompt_to_fix:
## Issue description
An invalid PIN response at the password step leaves the user on a form that can only resubmit the same permanently unusable credential.

## Fix Focus Areas
- sample_project_FE/src/pages/ForgotPassword.tsx[105-115]
- sample_project_FE/src/pages/ForgotPassword.tsx[225-253]

## Recommended Fix
Detect the backend's invalid-PIN response, clear the captured PIN, and return the user to a step where they can request or enter a new PIN. Preserve the password step only for failures that may succeed when retried unchanged.

still_open.title: Expired PINs trap users mid-reset

still_open.description: `resend` remains clickable while the PIN form is submitting, and every call to `requestReset` deletes the token currently being checked before issuing another. If a user resends while verification is in flight, verification can succeed against the old token before the resend commits, leaving the password step holding a PIN that the reset endpoint rejects.

diff_reference.code_snippet:
+            <button
+              type="button"
+              onClick={resend}
+              className="font-medium text-accent underline-offset-4 hover:underline"

evidence.explanation: The PIN form can start verification while the independent resend button can start another request, with no shared pending state. The backend deletes all existing tokens on each resend, whereas the frontend stores the previously verified PIN and later submits it to the reset endpoint.

fix_suggestion.prompt_to_fix:
## Issue description
The interface permits reset issuance and PIN verification to overlap even though issuing another PIN invalidates the credential being verified.

## Fix Focus Areas
- sample_project_FE/src/pages/ForgotPassword.tsx[93-125]
- sample_project_FE/src/pages/ForgotPassword.tsx[197-220]
- sample_project_BE/src/main/java/com/sampleproject/diary/service/PasswordResetService.java[68-75]

## Recommended Fix
Track resend activity and disable both resend and verification controls whenever either request is pending. Ensure only one resend can run at a time, and clear any previously accepted PIN whenever a new PIN is requested.

still_open.title: Resending can invalidate a valid PIN

still_open.description: `resend` starts another forgot-password request without recording an in-flight state, and its button remains enabled while that request runs. Multiple quick clicks create multiple reset requests, each deleting the preceding token, so a user can select an earlier delivered PIN that the newest request has already invalidated.

evidence.explanation: The new handler has no pending-state guard and the new resend button is always actionable. On the server, every forgot-password request deletes all tokens for the user before saving a replacement, so overlapping UI requests necessarily invalidate earlier PINs.

fix_suggestion.prompt_to_fix:
## Issue description
The resend action permits overlapping password-reset requests. Each request replaces the existing reset token, so a user can receive more than one PIN while only the latest token remains usable.

## Fix Focus Areas
- sample_project_FE/src/pages/ForgotPassword.tsx[117-125]
- sample_project_FE/src/pages/ForgotPassword.tsx[214-220]
- sample_project_BE/src/main/java/com/sampleproject/diary/service/PasswordResetService.java[68-75]

## Recommended Fix
Track resend submission state in the ForgotPassword component, return early when a resend is already pending, and disable the resend button until the request settles. Optionally render a loading label so the user knows the request is in progress.
